title: Episode 100: Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys: The Storming of Fort Ticonderoga
description:
In May 1775, Ethan Allen and his frontier militia, the Green Mountain Boys, joined forces with Benedict Arnold to execute a dawn raid on Britain's formidable Fort Ticonderoga, capturing the heavy artillery that would liberate Boston.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we journey into the rugged Green Mountains of Vermont during the electrifying opening weeks of the American Revolutionary War. Following the bloodshed at Lexington and Concord in April seventeen seventy-five, the fledgling American rebellion faced a desperate crisis: they had British troops besieged in Boston, but possessed no heavy siege cannon to dislodge them. Enter Ethan Allen, a six-foot-two frontier brawler, philosopher, and commander of the notorious Green Mountain Boys. In a daring midnight crossing of Lake Champlain alongside an arrogant Benedict Arnold, Allen bluffed his way into the 'Gibraltar of America' and demanded its surrender 'in the name of the Great Jehovah and the Continental Congress.' Here is George with the full, roaring account.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE OUTLAWS OF THE NEW HAMPSHIRE GRANTS
In the seventeen sixties and early seventeen seventies, the rugged wilderness between the Connecticut River and Lake Champlain—known as the New Hampshire Grants—was a turbulent frontier battleground. Settlers who had cleared timber and established farms under legal land grants issued by Royal Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire found themselves under threat of eviction by the wealthy, aristocratic land barons of New York, whose corrupt colonial courts declared the New Hampshire deeds null and void. When New York sheriffs rode into the valleys to seize properties, they were met by armed defiance from local settlers determined to defend their homes.
Leading this fierce resistance was Ethan Allen, a towering, charismatic frontiersman with a booming voice, a sharp frontier wit, and a taste for taverns and Deist philosophy. In seventeen seventy, Allen organized his neighbors into a loose guerrilla militia known as the Green Mountain Boys. Operating out of the Catamount Tavern in Bennington, Allen and his men waged a clever, low-casualty war of intimidation against New York authorities. They tarred and feathered corrupt New York surveyors, dismantled illegal cabins, and administered the 'beech seal'—severe floggings with stout beech switches—to New York magistrates who dared enforce eviction decrees.
The Royal Governor of New York placed a bounty of one hundred pounds on Ethan Allen's head, labeling him a dangerous outlaw and traitor. But to the frontier settlers of the Green Mountains, Allen and his brothers Ira and Heman were folk heroes: champions of ordinary pioneers against aristocratic privilege and legal extortion. Yet destiny had far greater battles in store for the Green Mountain Boys than chasing New York surveyors.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE DESPERATE NEED FOR CANNON
In late April seventeen seventy-five, express couriers galloped into the Green Mountains with electrifying news: on April nineteenth, Massachusetts minutemen had clashed with British regulars on Lexington Green and Concord Bridge. The Revolutionary War had begun. Thousands of colonial militia had rushed to Boston, trapping British General Thomas Gage inside the city. Yet the colonial army faced a fatal tactical weakness: while they held the hills surrounding Boston, they possessed virtually no heavy artillery capable of breaching British fortifications or driving the Royal Navy fleet from Boston Harbor.
Two hundred miles to the northwest, perched strategically on the narrow waters connecting Lake George and Lake Champlain in northern New York, stood Fort Ticonderoga. Built by the French in the seventeen fifties as Fort Carillon, Ticonderoga was known as the 'Gibraltar of America.' It had witnessed some of the bloodiest fighting of the French and Indian War, and though its stone ramparts had fallen into disrepair during years of peace, its bastions still housed over one hundred heavy brass and iron cannons, mortars, and coehorns, along with tons of precious gunpowder and musket balls.
Both the Connecticut Committee of Correspondence and a fiery Connecticut merchant named Benedict Arnold independently realized that Fort Ticonderoga was lightly garrisoned and ripe for the taking. Connecticut leaders dispatched funding and messengers to Bennington to recruit Ethan Allen and his Green Mountain Boys, knowing that no soldiers on the continent were better suited for a swift frontier raid through the primeval northern woods.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE CLASH OF EGOS: ALLEN AND ARNOLD
By early May seventeen seventy-five, over two hundred Green Mountain Boys and Massachusetts militia had assembled at Castleton, Vermont, eagerly preparing for the assault under Ethan Allen's command. Suddenly, an immaculate, elegantly uniformed officer galloped into camp accompanied by a single servant: Colonel Benedict Arnold. Arnold brandished a formal military commission from the Massachusetts Committee of Safety, authorizing him to raise troops and take supreme command of the expedition against Ticonderoga.
When Arnold announced his intention to assume command, the Green Mountain Boys erupted in furious rebellion. The rugged frontiersmen, clad in deerskin frocks and coonskin caps, laughed at Arnold's polished manners and swore with colorful oaths that they would fight only under Ethan Allen, whom they knew and trusted. They threatened to pack their knapsacks and march back to their farms if any Massachusetts stranger attempted to dictate orders.
Recognizing that the entire expedition was on the brink of falling apart before firing a shot, Allen and Arnold struck an uneasy, tense compromise. They agreed to march side by side at the head of the assault force, sharing joint command of the raid. It was an explosive partnership: two of the most aggressive, proud, and volatile military commanders in American history, united by a shared thirst for glory and a desperate prize across the water.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE MIDNIGHT CROSSING OF LAKE CHAMPLAIN
On the evening of Tuesday, May ninth, seventeen seventy-five, Allen and Arnold led their force through pitch-black forests to Hand's Cove, on the eastern shore of Lake Champlain, just two miles across the water from the stone bastions of Fort Ticonderoga. A violent spring thunderstorm was brewing; cold rain lashed the shoreline, and high winds whipped the dark lake into choppy, treacherous whitecaps.
The plan required ferrying two hundred men across the lake under cover of darkness before dawn. However, the expedition's boatmen had been able to procure only two small, clumsy flat-bottomed scows. Through grueling labor against heavy winds and waves, the rowers shuttled back and forth across the dark water, but as the hours slipped away, dawn began to break over the eastern mountains. Only eighty-three men—including Allen and Arnold—had landed on the western shore near the fort.
Allen knew that if he waited for the remaining boats to cross, daylight would expose their position to the British sentries, who could easily mow down the attackers with cannon canister shot from the ramparts. Gathering his eighty-three soaked, shivering men on the beach, Allen drew his sword and delivered a hushed, fiery address: 'Friends and fellow soldiers, we must quit our embarkations and march on the fort immediately. I will not compel any man to go contrary to his will. Those who will undertake to follow me in, poise your firelocks!' Every single man raised his musket without a whisper.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: 'IN THE NAME OF THE GREAT JEHOVAH!'
At three o'clock in the morning on Wednesday, May tenth, seventeen seventy-five, Allen and Arnold marched their eighty-three men swiftly toward the fort in two silent columns. They approached the south redoubt, slipping through an unfastened wicket gate in the exterior wall. A lone British sentry, startled by the dark figures emerging from the mist, leveled his musket at Allen's chest and pulled the trigger. The flintlock misfired with a harmless flash in the pan. Allen lunged forward, brandishing his heavy broadsword and striking the sentry with the flat of the blade, sending the terrified soldier fleeing into the interior parade ground.
Surging through the sally port with deafening war whoops, the Green Mountain Boys formed ranks in the parade ground, facing the barracks on all four sides. Allen strode directly to the wooden exterior staircase leading to the quarters of the fort's commanding officer, Captain William Delaplace. Pounding on the heavy door with the hilt of his sword, Allen bellowed for the commander to come forth instantly or have his entire garrison slaughtered.
A startled British officer, Lieutenant Jocelyn Feltham, opened the door in his nightshirt, frantically holding up his breeches in his hand. Staring in shock at the towering frontiersman and the armed men below, Feltham stammered: 'By what authority do you enter his Majesty's fort?' Ethan Allen raised his sword toward the heavens and delivered the immortal reply that became legend: 'In the name of the Great Jehovah and the Continental Congress!' Captain Delaplace then emerged and, realizing the fort was completely compromised without a chance for defense, surrendered his sword.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE PLUNDER AND THE NOBLE TRAIN OF ARTILLERY
The capture of Fort Ticonderoga was a flawless, bloodless triumph. Without losing a single soldier or firing a fatal shot, Allen and Arnold had captured forty-eight British soldiers, forty-four children and wives living in the fort, and an astonishing military arsenal: seventy-eight heavy cannon, six mortars, three howitzers, thirty thousand musket flints, and tens of thousands of cannonballs. To the immense delight of the Green Mountain Boys, they also discovered ninety casks of prime British rum in the fort's cellar, promptly staging a raucous, multi-day victory celebration on the ramparts that outraged the strait-laced Benedict Arnold.
Yet the true strategic significance of Ticonderoga's capture was realized six months later, in the dead of winter seventeen seventy-five and seventeen seventy-six. Twenty-five-year-old Boston bookseller turned artillery colonel Henry Knox arrived at Ticonderoga with orders from General George Washington to transport the fort's heavy artillery to Boston.
In an epic feat of logistical genius and endurance known as the 'Noble Train of Artillery,' Knox and his team selected fifty-nine heavy cannons and mortars, constructed forty-two massive wooden sledges, and hauled sixty tons of iron over frozen rivers, snow-drifted mountains, and rugged wilderness trails across Massachusetts. In March seventeen seventy-six, Washington mounted the Ticonderoga cannons atop Dorchester Heights overlooking Boston. Waking up to find American heavy artillery staring down their throats, the British army and Royal Navy evacuated Boston on March seventeenth, handing the American Revolution its first monumental strategic victory.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGACY OF VERMONT'S FOUNDING HERO
Ethan Allen's victory at Fort Ticonderoga established the Green Mountain Boys as one of the most celebrated and romanticized military outfits of the American Revolution. Just months later, in September seventeen seventy-five, Allen's reckless daring led him into disaster during an unauthorized assault on Montreal, where he was captured by British forces. For over two and a half years, Allen endured brutal captivity aboard British prison ships and in Pendennis Castle in Cornwall, England, before being exchanged in seventeen seventy-eight, returning to Vermont as a national hero.
Upon his return, Allen resumed his tireless fight for the independence of the New Hampshire Grants, helping forge the independent Republic of Vermont, which governed itself for fourteen years outside the United States. Allen published his philosophical masterpiece, 'Reason: The Only Oracle of Man,' along with a bestselling narrative of his captivity that captivated the young American republic.
Ethan Allen died suddenly in February seventeen eighty-nine, just two years before Vermont was admitted to the Union as the fourteenth state. Today, a monumental statue of Ethan Allen stands proudly in the National Statuary Hall of the United States Capitol in Washington, while the Vermont National Guard still proudly calls itself the 'Green Mountain Boys.' His audacious dawn raid at Ticonderoga remains an eternal symbol of American frontier audacity: the belief that courage, boldness, and love of liberty can overcome the mightiest empires on earth.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys handed the American Revolution its first heavy artillery, turning the tide at Boston. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we explore Vermont's fourteen years as an independent mountain republic.
